understand.restatement: Determine whether all brackets match by type and close in reverse order of opening, with no unmatched brackets left over.
understand.inputs: A string s containing only (, ), [, ], {, and }.
understand.outputs: A boolean: true if the string is well-formed; otherwise false.
constraints: Only the six bracket characters appear.
Input length is unspecified; aim for linear time.
Treat the empty string as valid.
clarifying_questions: Should an empty string count as well-formed?
What is the maximum input length?

examples.explanation: The square brackets close before the surrounding parentheses.
The ')' arrives while '[' is the most recent unmatched opening bracket.

pattern.name: Stack
pattern.why: The latest unmatched opening bracket must close first. Like Mira's nested gates in the story, each opening goes on top of a stack, and each closing must match and remove that top entry.
pattern.recognize: Use a stack when nested structures must finish in last-in, first-out order.

approach.brute_force: Repeatedly remove adjacent matching pairs: (), [], and {}. If a pass changes nothing, return whether the remaining string is empty. A valid nonempty string always contains an adjacent matching pair, but repeatedly scanning and rebuilding strings can take quadratic time.
approach.brute_force_pseudocode:
repeat:
    previous = s
    s = remove all occurrences of "()" from s
    s = remove all occurrences of "[]" from s
    s = remove all occurrences of "{}" from s
    if s == previous:
        return s is empty
approach.optimized: Use a stack to store unmatched opening brackets and a fixed mapping from each closing bracket to its required opener. Scan left to right: push openings; for a closing, reject if the stack is empty or its top has the wrong type, otherwise pop. Finally, accept only if the stack is empty. The stack always represents precisely the openings still awaiting closure.

complexity.explanation: For n characters, each character is examined once and each opening is pushed and popped at most once. Stack operations take amortized constant time. If every character is an opening bracket, the stack holds n entries. The brute-force method takes O(n²) worst-case time and O(n) working space.
follow_ups: How would you return the index of the first invalid bracket?
If the string contained only parentheses, could you use constant extra space?
How would you handle ordinary text and brackets inside quoted strings?

story.title: Mira and the Nested Moon Gates

scenes.caption: Mira enters the Moon Museum, where four glowing gate symbols line a corridor: (, [, ], ). Each opening leads into a smaller chamber. The curator whispers, “These gates remember your path.” Mira studies the symbols before stepping toward the first chamber.

To reach the moonstone, Mira must prove that every chamber closes with its own matching seal. She enters the round gate, then the square gate. “Square must close before round,” she realizes; leaving the outer chamber first would strand her inside the inner one.

At first, Mira copies the corridor onto parchment, erases neighboring matching symbols, and scans the whole drawing again. The square pair disappears, revealing the round pair. It works, but longer corridors demand exhausting rescans. “There must be a way to remember only unfinished chambers,” she sighs.

question.prompt: Why can repeated erasing become slow?
options: It may rescan the remaining string many times.
Matching pairs can never be adjacent.
It needs to sort every bracket.
question.hint: Imagine many parentheses nested inside one another.

scenes.caption: Mira returns to the original corridor with a pile of gate tokens: round below square. When the square seal appears, she checks only the top token and removes it. “Newest chamber first!” she cheers. A wrong seal, or a seal without any token, would stop her immediately.

question.prompt: After the square pair closes, which opener must ')' match?
question.hint: The square token is gone; look beneath it.

scenes.caption: The round seal matches Mira's last token, and the moonstone shines: no unfinished chambers remain. Her token pile is the code's stack, storing unmatched opening brackets. Push records an opening; top-check and pop verify a closing efficiently. One forward walk validates ([]), without repeatedly redrawing the corridor.

code_hotspots.why: The loop examines each character once unless a mismatch ends the scan early.
Each opening is appended once, using amortized constant time and potentially growing the stack to size n.
Each successful closing removes one opener in constant time.

frames.note: Start with no unmatched opening brackets.
Push '(' because it opens a new nested group.
Push '[' above '(' because it must close first.
The ']' matches the top '[', so pop that opener.
The ')' matches the remaining '(', so pop it.
The scan is complete and the stack is empty, so the string is well-formed.
